message.content:
A **1×1 convolution** (or 1×1 conv) is a convolutional filter with a spatial size of 1×1—essentially a dot product across the channel dimension at each spatial location (each pixel).

Even though it has no spatial extent, it is extremely powerful because it operates on the **depth** (channels) of the feature map.

### How it works
For an input feature map of size **H × W × C_in**, a 1×1 convolution with **C_out** filters produces an output of size **H × W × C_out**.

At each pixel (h, w), it takes the C_in-dimensional vector and multiplies it by a learnable weight matrix of size **C_in × C_out**, then adds a bias. It does **not** mix information across neighboring pixels—only across channels.

### Key uses

| Use | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **Dimensionality reduction / expansion** | Reduce or increase the number of channels (e.g., 512 → 64) with far fewer parameters than a 3×3 conv. |
| **Point-wise feature mixing** | Combine information from all input channels to form new features at each spatial point. |
| **Computational bottleneck** | In **Inception modules** (GoogleNet) and **ResNet bottlenecks**, 1×1 convs shrink channels before expensive 3×3 or 5×5 convolutions, cutting computation drastically. |
| **Channel-wise attention / gating** | Used in Squeeze-and-Excitation networks (SE blocks) and some normalization/attention mechanisms to learn per-channel weights. |

### Why it’s cheap
A standard 3×3 convolution on H×W×C has roughly **9·C²** parameters per output channel (ignoring input/output differences). A 1×1 has only **C²** parameters (or C_in·C_out), making it a lightweight way to rearrange and compress channel information.

**In short:** It’s a fully connected layer applied independently to each pixel, used widely to control model width/depth and mix cross-channel features without touching spatial structure.
